speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Surely it's a similar kind of thing.

text: But for security frameworks that exist in the real enterprise world, like SOC2, HITRUST, HIPAA, an audit trail is a bit more than that.

text: It has to contain a complete record of absolutely every action that the agent took.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It has to contain all of the places where the agent accessed data, all of the authorization by which the agent did something.

text: It's this complete record in a much more fundamental way.

text: And one way of thinking about it is in a legal sense.

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: When I think about architecting systems like this, I think often about what do I want to make easy.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: When I'm choosing my constraints, I'm saying, OK, these are the things I want my system to be easy, and let that drive the trade-offs that I'm going to make.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And a particular pattern that is used in lots of different industries, for example, in finance, is a transaction log, an immutable record of events that store all of the transactions that happen throughout the system.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And this is append-only, timestamp-log.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It's complete.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So this is your source of truth for all of the data of the system.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And it's unified.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So there is only one source of truth across all of the different agents that you might have running in parallel, for example.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And architecting this way, making this trade-off, means that auditability becomes trivial.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It falls out of your data storage paradigm that you've chosen.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It's impossible not to be able to roll back time and see exactly the state of the system at a particular point in time and be able to provide that as an audit trail for what happened at each point in time.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And of course, these are trade-offs.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So what's a trade-off you're making here?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: I think we could say that for this kind of event logging, or sometimes called event sourcing pattern, writes become very easy.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So you just drop an event.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Reads become more difficult because you have to read through all of the events in order to reconstruct a view of what happened.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And there are patterns like caching and snapshots that you can bring to make that simpler.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But there always is more effort there.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Although I have seen in the healthcare context that actually you're going to want different interpretations of the raw data that your agents recorded after the fact.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So for example, it might be that more events happened and that changes the interpretation of the healthcare journey and you want a different view of the source of truth at that particular time.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And this pattern makes that easy because all of your views of the data are ephemeral computed projections of the event log.

text: And so an architectural paradigm I might go to is object storage.

text: Schema-driven object storage I think is a good fit for this.

text: It matches well with the choice of using event logging because you can separate the two.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So the events we talked about as the record of what the agent is doing at any particular time only contain references to the schema-driven blobs that are the storage of the actual healthcare data itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And it's important, therefore, that the healthcare data is stored immutably, again, so that you can always go back in time and reconstruct what data the agent had access to at that particular point in time.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This separation of events for what happened and object storage for the data that was used at that particular point in time
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: has actually some very useful benefits.

text: For example, with a system like this, it's possible for developers to go back and debug and have observability over what happened, what particular steps the agent took, why it did that, and retrace the agent's steps without having access to the

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So you can separate out observability and orchestration and instrumentation from the healthcare data itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This then has another benefit, which is zero trust.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The object storage becomes a place where you can apply zero trust principles

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This then leads into a mitigation for prompt injection for the lethal trifecta.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And zero trust principles, tokens are bared by the agents, and object storage segregated from the event stream that has your orchestration logic gives you a place to be able to solve for that constraint.
speaker: SPEAKER_01
